- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

{"number":1112,"title":"Verify in production: a member's un-converged workflow still starts a scheduler run through the `tick.mjs` shim","body":"#877 renamed `engine/scheduler/queue/tick.mjs` to `scheduler-run.mjs` and left a shim at the old path (DESIGN decision 27, landed in #1108 / `a9a783e`).

**Why this could not be watched now.** The two halves of the change reach a member on different clocks. The mount refreshes on a converge; `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands later as a pull request somebody merges. The window this shim exists for — **new mount, old workflow, still naming `tick.mjs`** — therefore only opens once a member has converged, and is only exercised at that member's next hourly scheduler run. At the time of writing GoogleCalendarEventCreator had the old mount and the old workflow, so the window had not opened yet.

A synthetic version of it is already covered: the `old-workflows` rehearsal fixture converges a member holding the previous workflow shape, and `engine-tests/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run-entry-shim.test.mjs` pins that the shim starts the run and that `scheduler-workflow-shape` accepts either spelling. What no test can show is a real member's scheduler workflow running green through it.

If this fails, every member in that window has a queue that has silently stopped — nothing instantiates standing items, nothing readies blocked ones, nothing reclaims a dead claim — with no run left to report it.

Original-issue: #877
In-production-when: any member repo whose `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/scheduler-run.mjs` exists AND whose `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` still runs `queue/tick.mjs`. Read both files on that repo's default branch. If no member is in that state — every member either still has the old mount, or has already merged the new workflow — the window has not opened and this is not yet live.
Verify: that member's most recent completed `claudinite-scheduler.yml` run, started after the mount converged, concluded `success`, and its log carries the shim's own line `invoked as \`tick.mjs\`, which is the old name for the scheduler run`. A pass is that line plus a green conclusion. A failure is any conclusion other than `success`, or a run whose log shows the entry point could not be found.
Not-before: 2026-08-20T15:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

---

**Instructions for the run.** You decide nothing here; execute this playbook.

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real files on real member repos. Never infer it from a merge, a green canon run, or elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence you actually read — the member, the run URL, the log line — and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #877 with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by one day, re-apply `claude-task` and `claude-model:sonnet`, and leave this issue open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

One extra exit worth taking: if every member has merged its workflow pull request and none was ever observed mid-window, the window closed without incident. Say so, note that the shim's retirement condition (no member's workflow still names `tick.mjs`) is now met, and close this as completed.

[{"id":5356785448,"body":"Readings at 2026-08-20 13:52Z, right after the fleet-baseline sweep, so the run that picks this up starts from data rather than zero. Taken by cloning each repo's default branch and reading the two files.

| repo | mount has `scheduler-run.mjs` | workflow still names `tick.mjs` | state |

| ClaudiniteCanary | yes | no — it runs `scheduler-run.mjs` | **both halves converged**, `ref e3e0a91` |

So the canary went through in under ten minutes and no member was caught mid-window. That is consistent with it being the fastest-converging member by design, and it means the window is real but narrow — the three above have the old mount **and** the old workflow, so each will enter it when its mount lands and leave it when its workflow pull request merges.

Two notes for the run:

- **Do not read Canary as a pass.** It never sat in the window, so it proves the rename works on a real mount, not that the shim does. The assertion in the body is specifically about a repo holding the new mount beside the old workflow.
- The **window-closed-without-incident** exit in the body is the likely outcome if every member converges both halves as fast as Canary did. Take it — but only after confirming no member still names `tick.mjs`, since that is also the shim's retirement condition.

{"number":1113,"title":"Verify in production: members re-stamp with date-anchored versions","body":"#1105 changed `ENGINE_VERSION` and every pack's `version` from a plain integer to a date-anchored string (`'60820.1'`), and widened every reader to take both. What that changes for a member is the shape of a value in **its own** `.claudinite-checks.json` — the stamp the update flows write and the fleet surfaces read.

It could not be watched in the session that landed it, for one reason: a member's stamp only moves when that member converges, which happens on its own nightly cycle. The canary rehearsal ([run 32371130795](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32371130795)) did prove the path end to end — a legacy-stamped member through both flows, mount self-test green — but on **one** repo, against the branch. What is unproven is the fleet: that every member's next converge re-stamps rather than parking, and that a member sitting mid-migration (new engine, packs not yet updated) is not left in a state its own vendored readers reject.

Original-issue: #1100
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.claudinite-checks.json` on its default branch has `claudinite.engineVersion` matching `^\d{5,6}\.\d+$` rather than a bare integer.
Verify: read the same file on every member the fleet-roster tracker lists. Pass = every member's `claudinite.engineVersion` and every value in `claudinite.packVersions` is a date-anchored string, and no member has an open `needs-human` update PR whose reason mentions a version. Fail = any member still stamping a bare integer more than two of its own converge cycles after this landed, or any member parked with a version-shaped failure — name the member and quote the stamp.
Blocked-by: #1105
Not-before: 2026-08-22T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

**For the run.**

1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real file over the API. Never infer it from this issue having merged, from a green Actions run, or from elapsed time.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the stamps you actually read, member by member, and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #1100 with a comment saying what was asserted, what you found and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.

{"number":1126,"title":"Name the summary line in the session-start directive instead of pointing at it","body":"Fixes #1125.

`session-summary.mjs` printed the summary line, then a directive ending in "open your first reply of this session with **that line**". The directive was the last line on stdout, so the nearest line to the reply was the directive itself — and this session opened two replies in a row by reciting it verbatim.

Three properties now make the pick unambiguous, each pinned by the test:

- the directive **disclaims itself** ("an instruction to you, not text to repeat"), so it cannot read as the payload;
- **no deixis** — nothing points at a line the reader has to resolve;
- the summary line is emitted **once**, and **last**, introduced by the directive's colon, so recency now points at the right line rather than the wrong one.

Output is now:

```
SESSION-START SUMMARY — an instruction to you, not text to repeat. Open your first reply of this session with exactly this line, and nothing before it:

Claudinite loaded, 8 packs, 35 checks, 15,000 rule tokens, 23 available skills.
```

The existing test asserted the old deictic wording, so it is rewritten rather than added to — watched red on all four properties before the fix, green after. Nothing outside the loader parses this stdout, so the layout was free to change.

Full suite green apart from the shallow-clone guard in `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs`, which fails loudly by design in this sandbox's history-less checkout. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking.

{"number":1106,"title":"Remove the legacy single-integer version tolerance","body":"#1100 moved engine and pack versions to date-anchored `.` and left every reader accepting a legacy positive integer as well, parsed as `.0`. {"number":1094,"title":"Fleet grid: fold three columns, itemise the attention, count the tiles up","body":"Refs #1093. `claudinite-dashboard` v12 → v13.

### The five

**Count-up tiles.** A fleet load repaints on every member's read landing, so each headline number was rebuilt a dozen times in two seconds — you could not tell whether 7 became 9 or whether two different numbers were drawn. Only a number that *changed* tweens, a first paint appears, and `prefers-reduced-motion` gets the figure without the movement.

**A live rate pill.** `renderRatePill` ran once, before the sweep — so `60/60 · anonymous · cached 60m` was the budget from before every request that would have changed it. It now follows the budget as the sweep spends it (coalesced onto a frame; ~85 restatements per load would otherwise be ~85 layouts) and reports what this load cost. The *plan* is deliberately not re-decided mid-load — re-planning halfway would make a row's freshness depend on where in the sweep it landed.

**The explainer moved to the topbar.** It answers a question you have once, and as a `` in the flow it pushed the content it explains down the page on every load after that one.

**"Members need you" itemises.** `summariseMember` already separates a failure park from an inbox park from an approval park — the rollup was re-merging them into one word. The tile now reads `1 task broken · 1 item needing a decision · 3 items needing approval`. A kind nobody is waiting on is absent, not a zero.

**The member row gives back a column.** Stars fold into the member cell as `★ n` (they say what *kind* of repo this is, not whether it is healthy), CI reduces to a dot with its age beneath, and `Last commit`'s single "3h ago" becomes 90 days of GitHub-style commit squares. **1606px → 1438px, 13 columns → 12.** Measured in Chromium against a five-member fixture.

The graph is the one read on this page not derived from something already fetched, so it is priced as decoration: one `/stats/commit_activity` per member (52 weeks of daily counts in a single response), a 6h TTL, and not read at all once the policy drops below `tight`. Its three empty answers stay distinguishable — *not read*, *outside the reported year*, and *genuinely quiet* are three different facts and none of them is a blank square.

### The sixth was not a page bug

`▲ mount has not converged in 15 days` was v10 judging freshness on the stamp's `updated`, and v11 removed it. The report came from a deployment stuck on v10: the deploy fires `on: push`, but the pushes that move a mount are Claudinite's own auto-merged update PRs, and a push made with `GITHUB_TOKEN` fires no workflow. The seeded stub now also follows the vendored scheduler — a `workflow_run`, not a second `cron`, since the scheduler is a member's one permitted schedule — and asks an Actions cache entry keyed on the page's sources whether this exact tree is already live before building.

**`.github/workflows/` never converges, so this reaches new adopters only.** Shepherd's copy is missingbulb/Shepherd#106; any other existing deployment needs the same edit by hand.

### Also

`listRuns` was called with `30` by the fleet view and `40` by the repo view. The cache is keyed by URL, so those were two entries for one question — opening a member re-fetched the runs list the fleet page already held and kept a second near-identical copy in a ~5MB quota. Now one constant, with a guard against a caller passing its own page size again.

### Folders touched

- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — `ui.mjs` gains the count-up, the star mark, the CI dot and the commit grid; `github.mjs` the rate-change hook, `commitActivity` and the shared runs page size; `budget.mjs` an `extras` rung so decoration is what a tight budget drops first; `fleet.mjs` the park split in the rollup plus `attentionBreakdown`; `activity.mjs` the pure `commitDays` bucketing; `view-fleet.mjs` and `app.mjs` the wiring; `index.html` the header popover and the new cell styles.
- `packs/claudinite-dashboard/stubs/workflows/` — the deploy's catch-up trigger and its already-deployed gate.

### Verified

- The full suite: 2279/2280. The one failure is `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails on any shallow checkout by its own assertion and is untouched here.
- `check_the_world` 0 blocking; `check_the_work` clean.
- Driven in Chromium against a five-member fixture: the count-up sampled frame by frame (`0 → 1 → 7 → 13 → … → 30`, monotonic), the reduced-motion path confirmed to skip it, the pill confirmed to move during the sweep, and the grid measured before and after.
- The new guards were each watched to fail first — the runs-page-size guard against a reinstated `30`, and the scheduler-name guard against a misspelling.

One defect of my own turned up in that driving and is fixed here: a rAF callback is handed the timestamp of the frame it belongs to, which can predate the `performance.now()` taken while scheduling it, and a fractionally negative progress run through an ease that overshoots backwards drew the counter passing through **−12** on its way up from zero.

{"number":1123,"title":"No work, no item — the scheduler run decides at the anchor; declines live on the schedule board","body":"Implements #1115 as decided in the owner's 2026-08-20 comment: the scheduler run evaluates a task's precondition when its anchor comes and files a work item **only on a yes**; a no is a row on the one open `[claudinite-schedule]` board issue per repo; anything the scheduler cannot read fails **open** into an item the executor decides. The roll is gone: a pick-time no-go closes its item with the reason, and a one-time migration retires today's sleeping standing items onto the board.

Built simulator-first, per `sim/README.md`'s working discipline: the change was modeled in `sim.mjs`, the red tests named the scenarios it breaks, and prose + tests moved together.

## What changed

**Simulator** (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`)
- Evaluate-at-anchor in the modeled scheduler run; the board as a modeled **artifact** (rows the engine writes, a write log, absent/corrupt/refused-create degradations); the collapsed decline; the migration; force now mints when no item exists.
- New scenarios **S52–S60** (§L in SCENARIOS.md), covering: decline→row with lazy board creation, the watermark between anchors, deleted/corrupt board (one redundant ask, never a double run), per-task signal failure beside healthy tasks, the migration run twice and sparing blocker/first-ever waits, a decline racing a hand-minted item, write-only-what-changed, and a verdict flipping between anchor and pick.
- **F31, a real spec bug the sim caught before any engine code ran** (S60, watched red): a `go` row honored as a watermark eats the occurrence whenever the item's create fails after the row lands — fewer runs because a *write* failed, the inversion of fail-open. The watermark is therefore scoped to **declined rows only**; a go/fail-open verdict's cover is the item it created, judged by the occurrence guard. Ledger row added.

**Engine**
- `queue/schedule-board.mjs` (new) owns the board's parse/serialize/fetch the way `work-item.mjs` owns the item's schema: two-tier body budget under the ~64KB cap, per-row-tolerant parse (mangled ⇒ absent), oldest-open resolution, and *never write what could not be read* (an unreadable listing forbids the write so a blind create cannot mint a second board).
- `queue/scheduler-run.mjs`: `planSchedulerRun` becomes async and gains the injectable `evaluate(task)` seam + `board` input; only tasks at an uncovered anchor are evaluated; declined-row watermark; board rewritten only when an authoritative column changes, created lazily; the `retire-sleeping` migration op (idempotent — closed items never match, rows seeded only where absent; blocker waits and first-ever/adoption `Not-before`s untouched). The shell wires `collectSignalsForTask` + the precondition, failing open on a missing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`, a failed signal, or a throw.
- `queue/executor.mjs`: `noGoPlan`'s roll collapses into a close (`task:obsolete`, `not_planned`, reason in the close comment; a standing item's close points at the board). `Not-before` itself stays — it is still the blocked-item / request / first-ever mechanism. `rollBody` stays exported `@deprecated`: fielded rolls' bodies are stored data, and its round-trip test pins `parseLastVerdict`'s decode, which the migration and the dashboard read.
- `signals/index.mjs`: the `issues` collector's self-trigger exclusion becomes `/^\[claudinite-(task|work|schedule)\]/` **in the same change**, pinned red-green by a test — a board rewrite can never land in `issues.touched` and wake tidy-issues (the F8 class).
- Reader sweep for the new prefix: work-item family match / `listOpenWorkItems` / janitor are structurally blind to it (distinct prefix, distinct fetch path — each verified); `claudinite-dashboard`'s fleet-digest `isMachineIssue` learns it (as a literal, not a cross-lane import — #1004's skew class); the slot-mechanism sweeps match `[claudinite-task]` exactly and need nothing.

**Docs**
- DESIGN §5 **rewritten**, not amended: the "pure function of the clock and the issue list" rationale and the "issue list *is* the dashboard" cost bullet have lapsed and the section says so; the new invariant is stated (no durable scheduler state can silently eat a run — every board degradation resolves to one redundant evaluation, never a skip), with what the board is first authority for and why it is not the slot run-ledger returned. §15.28 records the decision with the four rejected alternatives from #1115. §2/§6/§8/§9/§14/§16.4 move with it; decisions 4 and 13 carry supersession notes; SCENARIOS §H is marked superseded record for the roll half; the coverage map gains the §15.28 row.

**Costs, named in §5**: signals collected twice for an occurrence that runs (the re-derive rule, paid only where work happens); a task whose signals need a credential the scheduler lacks pays one created-then-declined issue per occurrence (today: the two `fleet`-signal tasks) — accepted as the price of never skipping on a read failure.

## Verification
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`: **2383 pass, 0 fail** (sim: 69, incl. S52–S60).
- F31's sim test and the engine watermark test each watched red against the broken shape; the signals-regex pin watched red against the reverted regex.
- `check_the_work`: clean (pack versions bumped for the two touched packs). `check_the_world`: 0 blocking; the two advisory findings on touched files pre-exist on `main`.

Closes #1115.

{"number":1092,"title":"basics: a change proven only in production files its own verification","body":"Closes #1091.

Yesterday's flow is the motivation: the checkbox rule landed green, and whether it closed a real issue on a real repo took the owner asking. This replaces the asking with a mechanism.

**Reworked after review: skill only — the queue is the mechanism.** The first cut added a standing daily task; the owner pointed at the request lane, and it already carries everything: a marked issue is adopted, waits on `Blocked-by:`, and the mark is consumed at adoption so re-marking re-adopts — the whole retry loop in existing vocabulary. The bespoke task was a second queue beside it and is gone.

**The discipline.** At the end of every change, beside the conversation capture, a session runs the new skill unasked. Most changes file nothing — watched working this session, pinned by a test that ran, or having no observable effect at all (comments, design docs, a refactor a green suite already covers). What files something is the narrow case: the effect first appears in a place and at a moment the repo cannot see yet.

**What gets filed** is a deferred request, `/do-later`'s sibling: an ordinary issue marked `claude-task`, `Blocked-by:` the change's PR, `Not-before:` just past the expected release, carrying `In-production-when:` (an artifact to *read* — a member's stamp, a live version endpoint — never a duration), `Verify:` (an assertion with a pass condition), and `Give-up-after:`. The brief tells the adopted run how to converge: live and passing → close with the evidence read; live and failing → file the fault and close pointing at it; not yet live → bump its own `Not-before:` and re-mark, silently, capped at the give-up date, past which never-shipped becomes one comment and a close.

**One generic engine gap closed:** adoption now carries a still-future `Not-before:` from the marked issue onto the item, symmetric with the `Blocked-by:` carry (a past one is dropped like a closed blocker). Job 1 already honored `notBefore` on items — only the request-side spelling was missing, and without it a re-marked verification is picked within the hour, forever.

**Folders touched**

- `packs/basics/skills/verify-in-production/` — new skill: the discernment test, the request's shape, and the run's convergence rules.
- `packs/basics/` — `RULES.md`'s "when verifying now is genuinely impossible" bullet now routes to the skill; pack bumped to 13.
- `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` — the post-merge step, beside the conversation capture; pack bumped to 7.
- `engine/scheduler/queue/` — the `Not-before:` adoption carry in `tick.mjs`.

@@ -0,0 +1,88 @@
+---
+name: verify-in-production
+description: Decide whether a change that just landed can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use at the end of every change, beside the conversation capture — not on request.
+---
+
+# Verify in production
+
+A change is finished when someone has watched it work. Most changes you can watch **now**, and
+that is the rule — this skill is only for the rest: a change whose proof lives somewhere the
+repo cannot see yet. It fires **automatically at the end of a change**, unasked. You are filing
+the proof, not doing the work — and the proof itself runs unattended: an automatic check, end
+to end, with a person entering only where no automatic check can exist.
+
+## First: does this file anything at all?
+
+Most changes **file nothing.** Run the test in this order and stop at the first answer:
+
+1. **Did you watch it work in this session?** Then it is proven. File nothing.
+2. **Did a test that ran prove it?** A unit test, a CI job, an executable-requirements or UI
+   test covering exactly the behaviour that changed. File nothing — the suite is the mechanism
+   that comes back.
+3. **Does the change have an observable effect at all?** A comment, a design doc, a README, a
+   rename with no behavioural edge, a refactor a passing suite already pins. File nothing.
+4. **Otherwise: where does its effect first become observable?** If the answer is a place and a
+   moment — a member repo once it converges, a site once it deploys, a session once it reloads
+   its rules — that is what you file.
+
+The bar is *could not be watched now*, not *would be nice to double-check*. A verification
+filed for a change already covered by a test is a wasted run re-proving what the suite proved.
+
+## What you file
+
+**A deferred request** — the same ad-hoc lane `/do-later` rides, so the queue does the waiting,
+the running and the lifecycle; nothing here adds machinery beside it. One issue, titled
+`Verify in production: <the change, in a few words>`, its body the whole brief: the run that
+verifies will never see this conversation and may be days away. Say what changed and why it
+could not be watched now, then, each spelled verbatim on its own line:
+
+```
+Original-issue: #<the change's issue>
+In-production-when: <the concrete artifact to read, and what makes it true>
+Verify: <what to observe, and what counts as a pass>
+Blocked-by: #<the change's PR>
+Not-before: <ISO instant just past the expected release>
+Retry-every: <how far to push Not-before when not yet live, e.g. 1 day>
+```
+
+- **`Original-issue:`** is where a failure lands — the issue the change was done under, which
+  the run reopens if the verification fails.
+- **`In-production-when:`** names a thing to *read*, never a duration to wait. "`missingbulb/Shepherd`'s
+  `.claudinite-checks.json` stamps `packVersions.tidy-repo` at 8 or higher." "The live site's
+  `/version.json` reports a version past 4.2.0." "Any session started after this landed — check
+  the vendored copy under `.claudinite/shared/` carries the new text." A merge is not a
+  production condition, and neither is elapsed time.
+- **`Verify:`** is an assertion with a pass condition, not a topic — and a read an **unattended
+  run can make**: an API response, a file at a URL, an issue's state. "Issue #100 on that repo
+  is closed with a comment citing the ticks" beats "check tidy-issues works". Only where no
+  automatic check can exist may `Verify:` name a person's step, spelled out exactly.
+- **`Blocked-by:`/`Not-before:`** are the queue's own wait fields: adoption holds the run until
+  the PR has closed **and** the moment has passed. Aim `Not-before:` just past the release you
+  expect — the re-arm covers a miss, so don't pad it.
+- **`Retry-every:`** is the extension you are prescribing: when the run finds the change not
+  yet live, it pushes `Not-before:` forward by exactly this much. Size it to the release you
+  wait on — a nightly converge retries daily, a next-session rule in minutes.
+
+Then the labels, as `/do-later` applies them: **`claude-task`** (the mark the tick adopts) and
+**`claude-model:sonnet`** (reading a live artifact and judging an assertion against it). Never
+`claude-automerge` — a verification has nothing to merge. If `claude-task` doesn't exist in the
+repo yet, say so and leave the issue — the labels appear on the next tick.
+
+## Tell the run how to converge
+
+End the body with instructions to the run itself — the issue is its whole brief, and the run
+decides nothing: it executes this playbook.
+
+1. Read `In-production-when:` against the real artifact. Never infer it from a merge, a green
+   run, or elapsed time.
+2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the evidence actually read (the version, the value,
+   the URL) and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen `Original-issue:` with a comment
+   saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking
+   that; close this issue as completed — the verification did its job by finding the fault.
+3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, re-apply `claude-task` and
+   `claude-model:sonnet`, and leave the issue open — the next tick re-adopts it. No comment;
+   the bumped field is the record.
+
+## Then say what you filed
+
+One line back to the owner: the issue link, what it waits on, and its retry cadence.

@@ -0,0 +1,50 @@
+// The verify-in-production skill (#1091) rides the request lane — the queue is the
+// delayed-execution mechanism, so the skill's whole contract is prose. These pin
+// the parts the machinery depends on; the Not-before adoption carry it leans on is
+// engine behaviour, tested in engine-tests/scheduler/queue/request-mode.test.mjs.
+import { test } from 'node:test';
+import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
+import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
+import { join, dirname } from 'node:path';
+import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
+
+const skill = readFileSync(
+  join(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), 'skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md'), 'utf8');
+
+test('the skill carries the discernment test — most changes file nothing', () => {
+  assert.match(skill, /file nothing/i,
+    'the skill never says which changes file nothing, so every change would file one');
+});
+
+test('what it files is a request the queue adopts, not a mechanism beside it', () => {
+  assert.match(skill, /`claude-task`/, 'the mark is what makes the tick adopt the issue');
+  assert.match(skill, /Blocked-by:/, 'without the PR blocker the run races the merge');
+  assert.match(skill, /Not-before:/, 'without the delay the run fires before the release it waits on');
+  assert.doesNotMatch(skill, /claude-automerge.*apply/i, 'a verification has nothing to merge');
+});
+
+// The verification is AUTOMATIC end to end: the filed check must be one an
+// unattended run can read, and a person enters only where no such read exists.
+test('the check is automatic by construction, and a human is the last resort', () => {
+  assert.match(skill, /unattended[\s*]+run can make/i,
+    'nothing requires Verify: to be automatically checkable');
+  assert.match(skill, /no automatic check/i,
+    'the skill never bounds when a person may be asked at all');
+});
+
+// A failed verification routes back to the ORIGINAL issue — reopened, with the
+// status commented — so the filer's brief must carry that issue's number.
+test('a failing run reopens the original issue the filed brief names', () => {
+  assert.match(skill, /Original-issue:/);
+  assert.match(skill, /reopen/i);
+});
+
+// Not-live-yet re-arms silently, by the extension the FILER stated — the run just
+// executes its playbook, deciding nothing.
+test('a not-yet-live run re-arms by the filed Retry-every, mark and field only', () => {
+  assert.match(skill, /Retry-every:/);
+  assert.match(skill, /re-apply\s+`claude-task`/i);
+  assert.match(skill, /No comment/i);
+  assert.doesNotMatch(skill, /Give-up-after/, 'the give-up marker was dropped (owner, 2026-08-20)');
+  assert.doesNotMatch(skill, /sensible/i, 'the run decides nothing — the filer stated the extension');
+});

+# Merge to main
 
-The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.
+If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
+points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.
 
-**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.
-
-## Recipe (~4 calls)
-
-1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
-2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
-3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
-4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
+1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
+2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
+3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
+4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
+   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
 5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
-
-The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.
-
-## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)
-
-Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
-`node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later, in the conversation half of the repo's scheduled `growth-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass (the capture step's own pack owns that standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `claudinite-growth` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.
-
-## Don't
-
-- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
+6. Capture the conversation:
+   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
+   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
+   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it again.
+7. Run the basics pack's
+   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
+   It decides whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the
+   issue that comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.
+
+Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.

```
! could not reconcile label "claude-automerge": 404
```

Seen on `main`'s run [32368276774](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32368276774/job/96422660810) and on a branch run of #1089 at the same minute, so it is **not** from that PR — it is standing behavior on every run, and has been long enough that nobody reads the line any more.

`ensureLabels(gh, repo, [...QUEUE_LABELS, ...REQUEST_LABELS])` is the caller; `AUTOMERGE_LABEL` (`claude-automerge`) is in `REQUEST_LABELS`. The reconcile is fail-soft, which is why the run stays green — but the label is the asker's merge authorization (`MERGE_IF_NARROW`), read from a write-gated label at adoption. A label that cannot be reconciled is one that may not exist in the picker for a person to apply, which would make that authorization unreachable rather than merely unstamped.

Worth establishing before deciding the fix:

- whether the label exists on the repo at all, or the 404 is the *update* path failing on a label that does exist,
- whether the same line appears on members (it would be the same code, so probably),
- whether anything has ever successfully read `claude-automerge` off an issue here.

{"number":1107,"title":"writing-migration-plans: a migration's cleanup is filed, not phased","body":"Follow-up to #1100 / #1105, now retargeted to `main`.

The technique #1105 used is worth writing down, and the skill that should carry it is the one about ordering a plan's phases: **a migration's cleanup is filed as work that comes back on its own, never written as a later phase.** A cleanup phase falls due long after the run that would have done it ended, and nothing brings it back; filed as a queued issue in the same change that creates the thing it cleans up, the owner can forget about it, which is the point.

It goes in the destructive-step exception in §1 — the paragraph that already names the migration's tail — plus a clause on finding 3 in the review list. Five lines net.

*(First draft was a 38-line section with its own heading. The owner's read on it — "very verbose for [one sentence]" — was right, and the section is gone.)*

### What changed, by folder

- **`packs/basics/skills/writing-migration-plans/`** — the rule, in §1's exception and finding 3.
- **`packs/basics/`** — the manifest version, since a pack's content is delivered on it.

{"number":1073,"title":"Move the Chrome Web Store release pipeline into Claudinite tasks","body":"Tracking issue. The `chrome-extension` pack ships the store release as five workflows plus three composite actions, with a `store-release` task that only *dispatches* them. Move the work itself into task code-work.

> ### ⛔ Blocked on #883
>
> **Do not start implementing anything.** #883 changes the queue-engine contract this plan is written against. Phase -1 below must complete first, and the revised plan needs owner approval before any code is written.

> **Body repaired 2026-08-20**, before any implementation, per `writing-migration-plans`. The original is archived in a comment below; the comment trail holds the derivation and the review that forced these changes. **From the first commit onward this body is append-only.**

Follows #1069 / #1071, which established that the grounds for keeping a workflow are narrower than the corpus claimed: an Actions-only secret is reachable from code-work (`required_secrets`), an OIDC identity is a `permissions:` line, and a one-shot external effect is `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`. The only surviving ground is the Actions **composition model** — a `uses:` step. In this pipeline that is exactly and only the Pages deploy.

## Owner decisions

1. **The privacy-page refresh leaves the release path.** It renders `PRIVACY.md`, which changes on its own schedule, not on every store publish. It gets its own trigger — and that is what removes the last `uses:` from the release path.
2. **Human "bump version" merges stay manual.** Today a bump merge cuts the GitHub Release but does **not** upload to the store; a human publishes deliberately. The daily patch auto-release remains the only automatic path to the store.
3. **`store-publish` reads the store** to decide whether the latest release is live, rather than inferring from the version diff.
4. **Member cleanup is done by a session** (route c). The general "no automation can retire a workflow it once delivered" gap stays unfiled; no pre-flight push.
5. **The bump lands as a self-merging PR**, not a push to main — via `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` → `land-pr.mjs`, under the member's own `maintenance.delivery`.

## End state — three atoms, plus the privacy page

One operation per task, chained by preconditions rather than by ordering edges or parameters. Each precondition becomes true *because the previous task produced its output*.

| task | frequency | precondition | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `release-patch-bump` | daily | shipped paths changed since the latest release tag | patch bump, landed as a self-merging PR |
| `release-package` | manual | manifest version ahead of the latest release | build + cut the GitHub Release |
| `store-publish` | manual | the latest release is not live on the store | upload the prod zip |
| `privacy-page` | manual | `PRIVACY.md` touched, or woken | dispatch the Pages deploy |

The `manual` tasks are woken by the session that merges the bump PR — "bump version" lands via a normal PR and `LGTM` merges it in-session, so a witness is already present and no cadence is needed.

`on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` belongs on **`store-publish` alone** — the store upload is the one genuinely non-idempotent act. The decomposition makes every other stage self-healing: a torn run leaves the world in a state the next stage's precondition re-derives.

`expected_outcome: 'merged-pr'` on `release-patch-bump`. `required_secrets: ['CHROME_EXTENSION_ID', 'CHROME_CLIENT_ID', 'CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET', 'CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN']` on `store-publish`.

### What each piece becomes

| today | becomes |
|---|---|
| `chrome-extension-release.yml` (orchestrator) | deleted — the tasks own every trigger |
| `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` | split across the three atoms |
| `chrome-extension-create-package.yml` | `release-package`'s worker |
| `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` | `store-publish`'s worker |
| `deploy-privacy-page.yml` | survives, rewritten to be dispatchable; the one remaining `uses:` surface |
| `actions/read-release-config/`, `actions/bump-extension-patch/` | plain modules the workers import; the `action.yml` wrappers deleted |
| `actions/report-failure/` | deleted, with **no replacement** — a failing task parks `needs-human`, which is the error report |
| `release-workflows.mjs` conformance | mostly deleted; what remains guards `release.config`, not workflow shape |

## Phase -1 — revisit against #883 (blocking)

#883 implements the work-as-work amendments in `engine/scheduler/queue/`. Several of this plan's conclusions were reasoned against the pre-amendment contract and must be re-derived, not merely re-read.

- [ ] **Re-derive the leash conclusion.** The plan concluded "no split; `release-package` stays one task" from a 50-minute job budget shared across `maxItems` items. #883 retires `timeout-minutes ≤ leash` once heartbeat comments land, and re-sizes run timeouts to `maxItems` × the largest work bound. Long work stops being illegal, so the constraint that produced that conclusion no longer exists in the same form.
- [ ] **Re-derive the chain's latency.** The three atoms are chained by preconditions, each becoming true because the previous produced its output. Under today's engine each link waits a tick (~1h). #883's **self-re-dispatch** and **readiness re-check at close (F1)** are both aimed exactly at that — with them, the chain drains in one sitting. This changes whether the decomposition is cheap or expensive, and may change the `frequency` choices.
- [ ] **Re-check the `report-failure` deletion against the durable record.** #883 adds the `claudinite-task-exec` record plus artifact links to the terminal comment, noting that today *"an agentless run's only record expires with its Actions log."* All three release tasks are agentless. Confirm the park-plus-record is the whole replacement, since the deletion was decided before that record existed.
- [ ] **Account for the `prework` → work-step key rename.** #883 lists it as a fleet migration touching the vendored key in every member's task files, shipped with a compatibility window. Writing three new task declarations immediately before that rename means authoring them on vocabulary that is about to change; decide whether to wait, or to write them on the new key behind the compatibility window.
- [ ] **Re-check tick/drain decoupling against Phase 2.** The drain leaving the tick's concurrency group changes how a forced `wake` behaves during member verification.
- [ ] **Re-run the whole plan review** (the `writing-migration-plans` findings-by-cost sort) against the amended engine, then **get owner approval on the revised plan before any code is written.**

**Exit:** #883 closed, every box above answered in a comment on this issue, and the owner has approved the revised plan.

## Phase 0 — out-of-band setup

**Nothing outside the repo.** The four `CHROME_*` secrets already exist in member repos under these names; no new token grant (the executor already has `contents: write` and `actions: write`); Pages source unchanged.

There **is** a delivery dependency, but it is a Phase 2 entry condition rather than a human step — see Phase 2.

## Phase 1 — the PR stack (one review gate)

PRs 1–4 stacked, each based on the previous, reviewed together, merged base-first. **PR 5 is authored in the stack but held out of that merge** — it is destructive to the canon's own delivery surface, so it lands only after Phase 2 reads back true.

- [ ] **1. Two signal collectors, and `release.config` as a module.** Lift `read-config.mjs` out of the composite action. Add to the `release` collector: a `/compare/{latestTag}...{defaultBranch}` changed-files read, and a store live-version read. Both are required — a precondition receives only `(signals, packConfig)` (`engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:326-328`) and the scheduler's checkout is depth-1 with no tags (`claudinite-scheduler.yml:56`), so neither answer is otherwise reachable. **Try the unauthenticated store read first**; only if it is unstable do credentials enter the signal layer, and then via `ctx` (the `signals/local.mjs` shape), never `process.env` inside a collector.
- [ ] **2. The three task declarations,** with authoritative preconditions over those signals.
- [ ] **3. The three workers.** `release-patch-bump` writes through `deliver-generated.mjs` — nothing touches the drain's checkout.
- [ ] **4. `privacy-page`, and `deploy-privacy-page.yml` rewritten** — add `workflow_dispatch`, carry its own `permissions:`, drop the `./.github/actions/report-failure` reference (Phase 3 deletes that composite).
- [ ] **5. (held) Retire the pack's workflow surface** — the four stubs, the composite actions, the `release-workflows.mjs` conformance, and the canon's own orphaned `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*.yml` copies.

**Exit (PRs 1–4):** `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` green on `main`, and the four task declarations validate against `engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs`.

## Phase 2 — execution

- [ ] **Entry condition:** each member's executor carries the four `CHROME_*` names under `# claudinite:secrets`. The stamp edits `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, which `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write, so it travels the withhold lane and lands via an apply-stage session. Without this the first forced run parks "missing secrets" and reads like a failure.
- [ ] Drive the pipeline on `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`, waking each atom in turn.
      **Exit:** each task's item terminal, and the store shows a submission at the expected version.
- [ ] Repeat on `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.
      **Exit:** all three members' items terminal.

## Phase 3 — the tail (destructive; only after Phase 2 reads back true)

- [ ] Merge PR 5.
- [ ] Attach the three member repos to a session with push access; delete the four `chrome-extension-*` workflows and the three `.github/actions/` composites from each, one PR per repo.
      **Exit:** each member's `.github/workflows/` contains `deploy-privacy-page.yml` and no other `chrome-extension-*` file, and each member's next release item still converges terminal.

A straggler between Phases 2 and 3 is **benign**: a leftover orchestrator's `create-package`-on-push does exactly what `release-package` does, and it no-ops when the version is already released. Whichever runs first cuts the Release; the other declines.

## Risks

- **`readShipsReleasePipeline`** detects a publisher by the orchestrator's `name:` **or** `.github/release.config`. Deleting the orchestrator leaves the config as the only signal; exercise that fallback before Phase 3, not during it.
- **Latency.** The daily patch release is unchanged. A human bump's Release waits for a deliberate wake — which is decision 2, not a regression. Owner: a Claude Code session can attach the member repos and write `.github/workflows/` directly. The plan's Phase 3 assumed the only writers were the converge lanes, which cannot deliver there. That assumption was too narrow.

**Route (c): this session removes them.** Routes (a) and (b) as written are both superseded.

What that changes, and what it doesn't:

- **It fully covers the affected set.** Only the three existing members hold vendored copies — `missingbulb/GoogleCalendarEventCreator`, `TLDR`, `CrosswordChat`. Once Phase 1 deletes the stubs from the pack, a newly-adopting repo never receives them. So a session sweep over three repos is a complete answer, not a partial one that leaves stragglers for a standing mechanism to chase.
- **It does not need the withhold lane extended.** The `deleted`-list work in route (a) is no longer on this migration's critical path.
- **It adds a scheduling constraint.** The cleanup now happens *in a session*, so it cannot be left to converge on its own. It has to be driven in the same sitting that observes Phase 2, per basics' *Finishing a change* — watch it work now.
- **It stays last.** Phase 3 is still the tail: the workflows are what release the extensions until the task takes over, so deleting them before Phase 2 reads back true would break shipping. Ordering unchanged.

- [ ] Delete `chrome-extension-release.yml`, `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml`, `chrome-extension-create-package.yml`, `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` and the three `.github/actions/` composites from each, one PR per repo.

Reviewed against `writing-migration-plans`' findings-by-cost sort and against the tree. Three findings break the plan's central claims. I re-verified each of these myself rather than taking the review's word for it; all hold.

### 1. The authoritative precondition is not computable — blocks PR 1 and 2

The plan's central move. A precondition receives `(signals, packConfig)` and nothing else — `evaluatePrecondition` at `engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:326-328`. The `release` collector returns `latestTag`, `manifestVersion`, `shipsPipeline` only (`engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs:193-197`); `commits.touchedPaths` is bounded by the task's own window, not by the latest release tag. Adding `shipPaths` supplies the *filter*, never the *diff*. Nor can it be computed from the checkout: `claudinite-scheduler.yml:56` is a default `actions/checkout@v5` — depth 1, no tags — which is exactly why the workflow being replaced needs `fetch-depth: 0` (`chrome-extension-daily-release.yml:70-73`).

Worse than "needs more work": a windowed diff **loses the self-healing tag baseline**. A parked or failed cycle strands any change that ages out of the window, permanently, because nothing else records it.

**Change:** PR 1 adds a `release`-collector read of `/compare/{latestTag}...{defaultBranch}` changed files. Without it, drop the authoritative-precondition claim and say the worker stays the exact gate.

### 2. The manual-publish trigger is structurally unreachable, not preserved

Two independent breaks. The `wake` input carries task ids only (`claudinite-scheduler.yml:34-37`), and a wake-minted item gets the fixed `FORCED_WAKE_CONTEXT` (`tick.mjs:203-204`) — there is no channel on that lever for a tag. And the precondition is re-evaluated at pick, but preconditions never see Context. Republishing an existing tag is exactly the state where manifest == latest release and nothing shipped moved, so **a forced item would converge to a no-op every time.**

**Change:** design the path (a `manual` sibling task honoring Context, or `create-work-item --context` as the named lever) or record dropping it as a decision. Owner call.

### 3. The leftover orchestrator is not inert — it races the primary trigger

Every link of the inertness chain checks out, but the chain covers only the *task's own* bump commit. Trigger 1 is a **human** "bump version" merge, which carries no `[skip ci]` and fires the leftover orchestrator's `create-package` (`chrome-extension-release.yml:72-76`). That cuts the Release immediately; the task then reads manifest == latestTag and **never runs the store upload for that version.** Silent, nothing red.

**Change:** orchestrator removal (or deleting its `push:` trigger) moves into the same sitting as each member's Phase 2 observation, not after it.

### 4. PR 5 is destructive-before-observed (skill criterion 3)

The stack merges base-first before Phase 2 runs. PR 5 deletes the stubs and strips the conformance, so if Phase 2 fails on all three members the fallback pipeline has no delivery mechanism left. The plan applies "destructive last" to members but not to the canon's own delivery surface.

**Change:** PR 5 stays top of the stack, merged only after Phase 2 reads back true.

### 5. `deploy-privacy-page.yml` cannot be dispatched, and Phase 3 breaks it

"Survives, `workflow_call`-only, dispatched by the new task" is self-contradictory — the file is `workflow_call` only (line 28-29), and the dispatch API needs a `workflow_dispatch` trigger. PR 4 deletes its only caller. It also uses `./.github/actions/report-failure` (line 103), which revised Phase 3 deletes from each member.

**Change:** PR 4 rewrites it — `workflow_dispatch`, its own `permissions:`, no deleted-composite reference — and Phase 3's deletion list aligns with the rewritten survivor.

### 6. Phase 0 "Nothing" hid a real pre-Phase-2 dependency

`required_secrets` and the stamp are real, but the stamp edits `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, which `GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write — it travels the withhold lane and lands via an apply-stage session. No exit condition reads that back, so the first forced run on each member predictably parks "missing secrets".

**Change:** add a pre-Phase-2 exit — each member's executor carries the four `CHROME_*` names under `# claudinite:secrets`.

### Smaller, still worth fixing

- **`expected_outcome: 'none'` is a PR write ceiling** (`task-contract.mjs:52-55`), not a description of the write surface. Legal for a task that pushes to main and cuts Releases, but misleading; the plan should say so explicitly.
- **The worker's "check" phase vs. the precondition-only rule.** If finding 1 forces the diff back into the worker, the plan re-creates the split it claims to close. State which side owns it.
- **The 50-minute budget is the *job*'s, shared across the drain** (`claudinite-executor.yml:42`), not the task's. A long code-work starting late in a busy drain is killed by the runner mid-one-shot — making `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` routine rather than exceptional, and each kill halts that repo's releases until a human requeues.
- **The canon's own orphaned copies.** `.github/workflows/chrome-extension-{release,daily-release,publish-store}.yml` are the pre-vendoring "(reusable)" shape and are untouched by the plan. Fold them into PR 5 — the repo's rule pairs a stub edit with its canon copy in the same commit.
- **PR 5's "write the migration record"** is superseded by route (c) but never marked so.
- **Route (c) is asserted, not verified.** A one-file pre-flight push to one member before scheduling Phase 3 costs minutes and removes the assumption.

### Verified and correct, for the record

`local.mjs` reads `.github/release.config`; `commits.touchedPaths` exists; the executor grants `contents: write` + `actions: write`; no automation can delete a member workflow; `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` does what the plan claims; `frequency: 'hourly'` is legal.

Two owner decisions, and the design change they force. Supersedes the *End state* and *Trigger surface* sections of the body; the phases below replace Phase 1's stack and Phase 3's ordering.

### Owner decisions

1. **Human "bump version" merges stay manual.** Today a bump merge cuts the GitHub Release but does **not** upload to the store — a human runs publish deliberately ([chrome-store-releases SKILL.md:341](../blob/main/packs/chrome-extension/skills/chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md)). The original plan silently made that automatic. It stays manual: the daily patch auto-release remains the only automatic path to the store.
2. **The manual-publish path needs no parameter.** All three documented uses of `mode: publish` want "the latest release" or the privacy page — the first-publication bootstrap (SKILL.md:271-275, which is about the privacy leg and dissolves under the privacy-page decision), "a deliberate release now" (SKILL.md:341, *"blank tag = latest release"*), and re-running after a store rejection. No procedure passes an explicit tag; `auto_publish: false` appears in the dispatch inputs and in no procedure. So the scheduler's existing `wake` lever is sufficient — **finding 2 dissolves**, and no Context channel is needed.

### Revised end state — four tasks, one outcome each

The precondition-is-the-only-decision-point rule means one task per outcome, not one task with modes:

| task | frequency | precondition | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store-package` | hourly | manifest version ahead of the latest release | build + cut the GitHub Release. **No store upload.** |
| `store-release` | daily | shipped paths changed since the latest release tag | patch bump → build → Release → **store upload** |
| `store-publish` | manual | a release exists | upload the latest release to the store |
| `privacy-page` | manual | `PRIVACY.md` touched, or woken | dispatch the Pages deploy |

`store-package` declares `after: ['chrome-extension/store-release']` — a real read-what-it-produces edge, so the two cannot race on the same cycle.

`store-release` drops to **daily**. The hourly cadence in the original plan was bought solely for human-bump latency; decision 1 removes that need, and the corpus's own cadence rule says take it from how often the signal moves.

### Finding 3 re-assessed — the straggler really is inert, on correct grounds

With human bumps staying manual, a leftover orchestrator's `create-package`-on-push does **exactly what `store-package` does**, and `create-package` no-ops when the version is already released. Whichever runs first cuts the Release; the other declines. Benign duplication, not a silent skipped upload. The original inertness argument was right by accident and wrong in its reasoning; this is the reasoning that holds.

**Phase 3 stays last** (per the review's finding 4 on the canon side, not on the member side).

Owner review of the four-task table. Three corrections land; supersedes the table in the previous comment.

### 1. `store-package` is `manual`, not `hourly`

Hourly was polling for an event that has a witness. "bump version" lands via a normal PR (`packs/basics/skills/bump-version/SKILL.md`) and the merge happens **in a session** — so that session wakes the task, and no cadence is needed. A task polling for something a present agent already knows about is the cadence rule's own failure mode.

### 2. The three tasks were overlapping bundles, not three jobs

`store-release` = bump + package + publish; `store-package` = package; `store-publish` = publish. Two of them looked like duplicates because they *were* — the same atoms glued differently.

Rejected: an optional flag on one release flow. It is a decision in a later phase, which `writing-tasks` forbids outright ("the precondition is the ONLY decision point"), and there is no channel to set it — preconditions receive `(signals, packConfig)` and never see the item's Context.

Accepted: decompose to one atom per task, chained by preconditions rather than by a parameter.

| task | frequency | precondition | does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `release-patch-bump` | daily | shipped paths changed since the latest release tag | patch bump + push |
| `release-package` | manual | manifest version ahead of the latest release | build + cut the GitHub Release |
| `store-publish` | manual | the latest release is not live on the store | upload the prod zip |

Each precondition becomes true **because the previous task produced its output**, so the pipeline is expressed as preconditions rather than as ordering — no `after:` edge, no shared code between tasks, and each task has exactly one outcome.

`store-package` never touched the store. `create-release-artifact` was proposed; rejected on basics' naming rule — "artifact" is the mechanism, and the responsibility is cutting a Release. The decomposition renames it anyway: `release-package`.

### Open: how `store-publish` knows, and how a deliberate publish gets through

Decision 1 (human bumps stay manual) means `store-publish` must not auto-fire after a minor/major bump. The structural read is available — the standard already draws patch-vs-deliberate (`chrome-store-releases/SKILL.md:43-46`) — so it could be inferred from the version diff with no state.

Owner decision: the precondition reads the store's live version rather than inferring from the version diff. Structural, no state, and a deliberate wake passes because the answer is genuinely "not live yet".

Checked what that costs, since PR 1 would otherwise discover it:

**It fits the collector model.** A collector is `async (gh, ctx)` (`engine/scheduler/signals/index.mjs:281-295`) — it may await anything, not only `gh`. ### Settled

- **The workflow-retirement gap stays unfiled.** A session can write member workflows, so it is not load-bearing. Route (c) stands.
- **No route (c) pre-flight.** The capability is confirmed by the owner; Phase 3 plans on it without a trial push.

### A property the decomposition bought, worth recording

The review's partial-state worry — interrupted between the bump push and the store upload — **stops being a failure mode**. With three atoms, an interrupted `release-patch-bump` leaves main bumped; `release-package` then sees manifest-ahead and cuts the Release on its next pick; `store-publish` then sees a release not live and uploads. Each stage's precondition re-derives the world, so a torn run heals on the next tick instead of needing `on_interrupt` to catch it. `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'` is still right on `store-publish` alone — the store upload is the one genuinely non-idempotent act.

### Still soft — needs deciding before PR 1

**1. `release-patch-bump` mutates the executor's shared checkout.**
The executor drains up to `DEFAULT_MAX_ITEMS = 3` items from one checkout (`engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs:29`). A worker that commits a version bump leaves the next item a tree it did not expect — precisely the failure the repo's own rule about one drain serving several items names. All three release tasks can be picked in the same drain, and two of them mutate the tree.

The constraint is real either way; the question is which shape: leave the tree clean after pushing (commit → push → reset hard), or do the bump in a temp clone and never touch the drain's tree at all. The second is more code but cannot leak.

**2. What replaces `report-failure` is not equivalent — and may be better.**
Today it opens **one dated issue per failure**, deduping earlier open ones for the same workflow, labeled `workflow-failure` (`stubs/actions/report-failure/action.yml:8-9, 70-74`). That is a durable human-facing artifact outside the queue.

A `needs-human` park is a work item, not a standing tracker — but a `failure` park **holds the task's lane**: no further occurrence is filed until it is woken or closed. That is a stronger guarantee than the dated issues, which accumulate while the pipeline keeps running into the same wall. So the replacement is not lossy; it trades an accumulating log for a stop-the-line. Worth confirming that is the intent rather than assuming it.
